claims.text: HEA protective-coating wear performance is governed primarily by microstructural homogeneity.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases and promoting a single-phase solid solution enhances coating toughness.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases and promoting a single-phase solid solution increases resistance to crack propagation during wear.
The initial HEA coating contains both single-phase solid-solution regions and intermetallic precipitates.
Controlled heat treatment can promote a more homogeneous single-phase solid solution or increase intermetallic-phase formation.
The fraction and distribution of intermetallic phases relative to the single-phase solid solution mediate wear performance.
A single-phase solid-solution microstructure increases toughness and ductility.
Increased toughness and ductility reduce crack initiation and propagation during wear.
Intermetallic phases act as brittle sites.
Brittle intermetallic sites accelerate material removal during wear.
Coatings with a more homogeneous single-phase solid solution will have lower wear rates than coatings with increased intermetallic content.
Coatings with a more homogeneous single-phase solid solution will show less surface damage than coatings with increased intermetallic content.
The hypothesis is expected to apply when constituent elements are mutually soluble and intermetallic formation is tunable through processing.
The hypothesis may not apply when intermetallic phases are inherently stable or dominant.
Equal or better wear performance from the intermetallic-rich coating would falsify the proposed superiority of the single-phase coating.
